lead: A switch closes and a circuit that was sitting still starts to move. This unit works out that movement — the first microseconds and the seconds after — for RL, RC and RLC circuits, first with differential equations and then with the Laplace transform. After it you can find initial conditions, write and solve the response of first- and second-order circuits, and read a transfer function's poles and zeros.
about: This unit is about what a circuit does in the moments after a switch moves. Chapter 5.1 fixes the starting values, 5.2 shows the free decay of one storage element and the time constant, and 5.3 adds a step source and splits the answer into natural and forced parts. Chapters 5.4 and 5.5 handle two storage elements, the three damping cases, ω_n and ζ. Chapter 5.6 keeps a sine source and shows the transient riding on the steady-state wave. Chapter 5.7 replaces all the differential equations with the Laplace transform, 5.8 turns the s-domain answer into a transfer function with poles and zeros, and 5.9, taught at only a few universities, writes the same circuit as state equations.

chapters.idea: Inductor current and capacitor voltage cannot jump, so the state at t = 0⁻ fixes the whole answer after switching.
chapters.depth: Switching at t = 0 and the notation t = 0⁻, t = 0⁺. Why i_L and v_C are continuous: the stored energy ½Li² and ½Cv² cannot change in zero time. The equivalent circuit at t = 0⁺ — inductor replaced by a current source of value i_L(0⁻), capacitor by a voltage source of value v_C(0⁻). The circuit at t = ∞ — inductor a short, capacitor an open. The one-step derivative values v_L(0⁺)/L and i_C(0⁺)/C. Some syllabi call this switching behaviour of R, L and C. Keep the excitation DC here.

figure.title: Conditions around the switch

nodes.label: t = 0⁺
nodes.note: L as current source, C as voltage source

figure.aria: Flow from the steady state before switching, through the switch event, to the equivalent circuit just after switching and then the final steady state.

chapters.example: A 12 V DC source, a switch, R = 6 Ω, L = 2 H and C = 0.5 F are in series. Nothing is stored before t = 0 and the switch closes at t = 0. Find i(0⁺), v_C(0⁺), di/dt at 0⁺, i(∞) and v_C(∞). Answer: i(0⁺) = 0 A, v_C(0⁺) = 0 V, di/dt(0⁺) = 12/2 = 6 A/s, i(∞) = 0 A, v_C(∞) = 12 V.
chapters.trap: Treating the inductor as an open circuit or the capacitor as a short circuit at t = 0⁺. The short/open rule belongs to t = ∞ and to the DC steady state only.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: V-I relations of R, L and C; KVL and KCL.
chapters.leave: The full solution of the equations — that is Chapters 5.2 to 5.4.

chapters.idea: With no source, stored energy drains through R as a pure exponential whose speed is set by the time constant τ.
chapters.depth: Source-free RL with τ = L/R and source-free RC with τ = RC. The decay x(t) = x(0)e^(−t/τ) and what τ means: the time to fall to 37 % (1/e) of the start. The initial-slope tangent meeting zero at t = τ, and the 5τ rule for 'practically zero'. Energy ½Li² or ½Cv² burnt in R. Why a large R makes an RL decay fast but an RC decay slow. Some syllabi head this natural response, or free response.

figure.aria: A decaying exponential with a straight tangent from the starting point that reaches zero exactly one time constant later.

chapters.example: An inductor L = 0.5 H carrying 2 A is connected across R = 100 Ω at t = 0. Find τ, i(t), and the time to reach 0.2 A. Answer: τ = L/R = 0.005 s = 5 ms, i(t) = 2e^(-200t) A, and t = τ ln 10 = 11.5 ms.
chapters.trap: Writing τ = R/L for an RL circuit or 1/(RC) for an RC circuit. τ must come out in seconds — check the units.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: V-I relations of L and C; Chapter 5.1 for the starting value.
chapters.leave: Driven circuits — step sources in Chapter 5.3, sine sources in Chapter 5.6.

chapters.idea: Any first-order answer is complete response = natural (decaying) part + forced (steady-state) part, and one formula joins the two end values.
chapters.depth: Step response of RL and RC with a DC source. Natural response (transient, homogeneous, complementary) plus forced response (steady state, particular). The single-line shortcut x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ), and how to use it for both current and voltage once τ and the two end values are known. Sketching from the start value, the end value and the initial slope. Rising and falling steps; what a pulse does in the same circuit at a high level.

figure.aria: The flat forced response and the decaying natural response adding up to the rising exponential of the total step response.

chapters.example: R = 50 kΩ and C = 2 μF are in series with a 10 V step applied at t = 0; the capacitor is uncharged. Find v_C(t), i(t) and v_C at t = 0.1 s. Answer: τ = RC = 0.1 s, v_C(t) = 10(1 − e^(-10t)) V, i(t) = 0.2e^(-10t) mA, v_C(0.1) = 6.32 V.
chapters.trap: Assuming the current and the capacitor voltage have the same end values. Capacitor voltage ends at the source value, its current ends at zero — and the current is the one that jumps.
chapters.leave: Second-order circuits in Chapter 5.4 and the s-domain route in Chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: Two storage elements give a quadratic characteristic equation, and its roots decide whether the answer creeps, just settles, or rings.
chapters.depth: Series and parallel RLC with a DC step. Characteristic equation s² + 2αs + ω₀² = 0, with α = R/(2L) for series and α = 1/(2RC) for parallel, and ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Three cases: α > ω₀ overdamped (two real roots), α = ω₀ critically damped (repeated root), α < ω₀ underdamped (complex roots, ringing). The shape of each solution, the constants fixed by v_C(0) and i_L(0), and sketches of v_C against time. Some syllabi say over-, critical- and under-damped response.

figure.aria: Three step responses of the same second-order circuit: one overshoots and rings, one rises as fast as possible without overshoot, one creeps up slowly.

chapters.example: A series RLC has L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F and a 10 V step source. Take R = 4 Ω, then 20 Ω, then 40 Ω. Find ω₀, α and the case for each. Answer: ω₀ = 1/√(LC) = 10 rad/s and α = R/(2L) = R/2 gives 2, 10 and 20 s⁻¹, so ζ = 0.2 underdamped, ζ = 1 critical, ζ = 2 overdamped. For R = 4 Ω, ω_d = √(100 − 4) = 9.8 rad/s.
chapters.trap: Using α = 1/(2RC) for a series circuit, and comparing α with ω₀ directly instead of α² with ω₀².
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.3 and Unit 1; Unit 4 for the resonance language.
chapters.leave: Naming the cases with ζ and ω_n and the design formulas — Chapter 5.5.

chapters.idea: Two numbers, ω_n and ζ, describe every second-order circuit: how fast it wants to oscillate and how strongly that oscillation is killed.
chapters.depth: Definitions ω_n = 1/√(LC) and ζ = α/ω_n, where α is R/(2L) for series and 1/(2RC) for parallel. Roots s = −ζω_n ± jω_n√(1 − ζ²); damped frequency ω_d = ω_n√(1 − ζ²). Percentage overshoot e^(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)), peak time π/ω_d, 2 % settling time about 4/(ζω_n), and Q = 1/(2ζ). The s-plane picture: poles moving on a circle of radius ω_n as ζ changes. Some syllabi use ω₀ for ω_n and call ζ the damping factor.

figure.aria: A classification of second-order behaviour branching from the value of the damping ratio into undamped, underdamped, critically damped, overdamped and unstable.

chapters.example: A series RLC has R = 20 Ω, L = 0.1 H, C = 10 μF and a 10 V step. Find ω_n, ζ, ω_d, peak overshoot, peak time and 2 % settling time. Answer: ω_n = 1000 rad/s, α = R/(2L) = 100 s⁻¹, ζ = 0.1, ω_d = 995 rad/s, overshoot = e^(−0.3157) = 72.9 %, t_p = π/995 = 3.16 ms, settling ≈ 4/100 = 40 ms.
chapters.trap: Writing ω_d = ω_n√(ζ² − 1), which is imaginary for ζ < 1, or feeding the parallel-RLC α into a series circuit.
chapters.leave: Resonance curves, bandwidth and Q as a steady-state idea — Unit 4. The s-plane reading of poles — Chapter 5.8.

chapters.idea: With a sine source the answer is a steady-state sine plus a decaying exponential, and the exponential's size depends on the instant of switching.
chapters.depth: RL and RC driven by v = V_m sin(ωt + φ). Steady-state part from the phasor of Unit 3, natural part K e^(−t/τ), total i(t) = I_m sin(ωt + φ − θ) + K e^(−t/τ) with K fixed by i(0⁺). Worst switching instant (source at a peak) versus the gentlest (source through zero at switching). The transient is gone in about 5τ. One line on RLC under AC: the steady state is still a phasor, the transient is now second order. Some syllabi call this transient response under AC excitation.

figure.aria: A steady sine, a decaying exponential and their sum: the total current starts at zero and settles onto the sine within a few time constants.

chapters.example: R = 4 Ω and L = 1 H are in series with v_s = 10 sin 3t V, and i(0) = 0. Find i(t). Answer: Z = 4 + j3 Ω, |Z| = 5 Ω, θ = 36.9°, steady state 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) A, τ = L/R = 0.25 s. At t = 0 the sine part equals −1.2 A, so K = 1.2 and i(t) = 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) + 1.2e^(−4t) A.
chapters.trap: Finding the phasor answer and stopping there. The constant K must come from the total current at t = 0⁺, not from the steady-state current.
chapters.leave: Full RLC-under-AC solutions and the Laplace shortcut of Chapter 5.7.

chapters.idea: The Laplace transform turns the differential equation into algebra and carries the initial conditions inside the circuit as extra sources.
chapters.depth: The one-sided transform, the pairs you need (1 → 1/s, e^(−at) → 1/(s+a), the derivative rule with f(0⁻)), and the initial and final value theorems. s-domain element models: R, sL with a series source L i_L(0⁻), 1/sC with a series source v_C(0⁻)/s. Building the transformed circuit, solving by nodal or mesh analysis in s, splitting with partial fractions, and taking the inverse transform. The answer must agree with the time-domain method of Chapters 5.3 and 5.4.

figure.title: Solving a transient in the s-domain
figure.aria: A pipeline that starts from the time-domain circuit, transforms each element, solves algebraically in s and inverts the answer back to time.

chapters.example: A 10 V DC source feeds R = 5 Ω and C = 0.1 F in series, and the capacitor is charged to 4 V before t = 0 when the source is connected. Find i(t) and v_C(t) using Laplace. Answer: I(s) = (10/s − 4/s)/(5 + 10/s) = 1.2/(s + 2), so i(t) = 1.2e^(−2t) A and v_C(t) = 10 − 6e^(−2t) V; check v_C(0⁺) = 4 V and v_C(∞) = 10 V.
chapters.trap: Getting the sign or the 1/s factor of the initial-condition source wrong. The error is silent — it shows up only when you check the answer at t = 0⁺.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (nodal and mesh analysis) and Chapter 5.1 (initial conditions).
chapters.leave: Transfer functions and poles — Chapter 5.8. The impulse response as a system property — also Chapter 5.8.

chapters.idea: With sources killed and zero initial energy, the circuit is just a ratio H(s) whose poles give the natural response and whose zeros shape the steady-state response.
chapters.depth: Driving-point and transfer functions; H(s) = output/input with all independent sources killed and initial conditions zero. Numerator roots are zeros, denominator roots are poles; the pole-zero plot in the s-plane. The impulse response as the inverse transform of H(s); H(jω) as the sinusoidal steady-state ratio and the peak near a pole close to the jω axis, tying back to Q in Unit 4. Stability: poles in the left half plane only. A pole on the jω axis means sustained oscillation, a pole on the right means growth.

figure.aria: Two magnitude curves of the same second-order low-pass function: the lightly damped one peaks sharply near ω = ω₀, the more damped one stays flat.

chapters.example: A series RLC has L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F and the output is taken across C. Find H(s), its poles and zeros, and the peak magnitude for R = 2 Ω and R = 10 Ω. Answer: H(s) = 100/(s² + (R/L)s + 100). For R = 2 Ω, poles at −1 ± j9.95, ζ = 0.1, |H| peaks at 5 when ω = 10 rad/s. For R = 10 Ω, poles at −5 ± j8.66, ζ = 0.5, peak |H| = 1. No finite zeros.
chapters.trap: Calling a pole on the jω axis stable, or reading stability from the zeros. Only pole positions decide stability; zeros only shape the size of the response.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.7; Unit 4 for resonance and Q.
chapters.leave: General stability theory beyond left-half-plane poles, and two-port transfer functions — Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Store the energy variables as one vector x and the whole circuit collapses into two matrix equations, ẋ = Ax + Bu and y = Cx + Du.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short and practical. State variables are the inductor currents and capacitor voltages — exactly the quantities that cannot jump. Number them x₁, x₂, …, write KVL and KCL until each derivative appears alone, and read off A, B, C, D. The eigenvalues of A are the natural frequencies, so no solving is needed to know whether the circuit rings. The integrator block diagram as the picture of the equations.

figure.title: State equations as a block diagram
figure.aria: Inputs enter through matrix B, add to the fed-back state through A, pass through integrators to give the state vector, and reach the output through C.

chapters.example: A series RLC has R = 1 Ω, L = 1 H, C = 1 F, input v_s and output v_C. Take x₁ = i_L and x₂ = v_C. Write A, B, C, D and the natural frequencies. Answer: di/dt = −i − v_C + v_s and dv_C/dt = i, so A = [[−1, −1], [1, 0]], B = [[1], [0]], C = [0 1], D = [0]. The eigenvalues solve s² + s + 1 = 0, giving s = −0.5 ± j0.866.
chapters.trap: Choosing a resistor voltage or a capacitor current as a state variable. The two states must be the two energy-storing quantities i_L and v_C.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 5.4 and basic matrix algebra; Chapter 5.8 for the transfer-function view.
chapters.leave: Hand solution of the matrix equations and the state-transition matrix — not needed for this unit's exams.
